claims.text: The starting eutectic high-entropy alloy has a hierarchical microstructure of dual-phase lamellar colonies.
The untreated alloy has limited room-temperature tensile ductility and inherent brittleness.
Dislocation pile-ups at internal or colony boundaries cause localized stress concentrations and brittleness in the untreated alloy.
The proposed intervention is approximately 30% cold rolling at room temperature followed by annealing at approximately 600°C for 10 minutes.
The proposed treatment will induce a high density of nano-twins within grains and near lamellar interfaces.
The induced nano-twins will form additional internal boundaries that act as dislocation barriers.
The induced nano-twins will act as dislocation sinks that absorb and redistribute dislocations during deformation.
Dislocation absorption and redistribution by nano-twins will reduce stress concentrations associated with dislocation pile-ups.
Reducing localized stress concentrations will mitigate microcrack initiation at lamellar interfaces.
Nano-twins will improve strain accommodation and delay crack initiation.
The treatment will increase elongation to failure relative to the untreated alloy.
The treatment will maintain or marginally increase yield strength and ultimate tensile strength relative to the untreated alloy.
Work hardening enabled by the nano-twinned structure will preserve or enhance strength.
The predicted improvement applies under quasi-static tensile loading at room temperature.
Similar thermomechanical processes in comparable alloys have shown promise.

contradictions.description: Nano-twins are described both as dislocation sinks that absorb dislocations and as barriers that obstruct dislocation motion. These roles are not necessarily mutually exclusive, but the hypothesis does not explain how the same twin population performs both functions without promoting new pile-ups.

The prediction requires strength to be maintained or only marginally increased, whereas the falsification rule initially demands a statistically significant increase in both ductility and strength but then treats no strength reduction as sufficient. A statistically significant strength increase and mere strength retention are different criteria.
